column8: Promoting cyber awareness to the wider business
column10:
6.	At [company] we had a CyPOC (Cyber Point of Contact) program that looked to promote cybersecurity within their part of the organisation. It hadn’t been a success, and when I suggested we rebrand and relaunch it, it was met by a lack of interest in many quarters. I persevered and argued that we needed to make it personal for it to succeed. I referenced how, when I was in the military, I was the qualified first aider in the team. There was an opportunity for others to get trained up, but there were no volunteers. Their reasoning was that they didn’t want the responsibility if someone keeled over, or they didn’t like blood/vomit, or they might get promoted if I collapsed and died (I’ve always hoped that last one was a joke). I countered that if, in a few months’ time, their parent collapsed and stopped breathing, or their child began choking on something, or their partner had an accident at home, how would they feel, standing there, knowing that they could have received free training that would have put them in a better position to help? This resulted in several of them applying for the first aid course. So, my philosophy for cybersecurity awareness is that you must make it personal. People aren’t that bothered about the business, but if you say that you will teach them skills that will make them and their family more secure online, and it’s free, they are more likely to commit. They become more cyber aware and that enhances the cyber maturity within their team. I managed to get a few interested colleagues onboard, and the CISO signed it off. 
About the same time, a member of [company] had been the victim of a cyberattack at home. This resulted in all the family accounts online being compromised (banks, insurance, gaming platforms, NHS, social media, streaming services, etc.). They didn’t know where to turn, so he turned to his line manager, who turned to the CISO, who turned to me. We helped give him some advice and pointed him to some agencies that could help him, including the police. He was an emotional wreck and had even had the hacker phone him at home to demand £500! So now we had evidence that ransomware attacks could happen to the individual. That it’s not just a business thing. He eventually got his life back with the help of a detective sergeant who spent time with him and his family in their home to get his accounts sorted and hardened.  I asked if he was willing to share his very personal story at our Cyber Awareness month, and he was enthusiastic to do so. He ran a session with the Det Sgt, him explaining the personal trauma, while she promoted how to best keep you and your family safe online. We promoted it and it was the most watched event that year. It was recorded, and word of mouth meant it continued being viewed weeks later. It also resulted in a significant uptick in applications to our newly revamped “cyber champions” program. So, making it personal is proven to have more impact than suggesting individuals would want to protect the business.

Input from a broad range of specialisms and from senior levels in the consultancy was needed to persuade the client that the external-only constraint would limit the value of the exercise, and that ‘assumed breach’ and/or ‘insider threat’ scenarios were realistic, legitimate concerns.
